title: Silent Endings · The -ent of {ils veulent}
description: Say the {ils} and {elles} form of a verb without its -ent, and see why it stays in writing.
can_do: Say {ils veulent} and {elles veulent} without the -ent.
Tell {il veut} from {ils veulent} by the l you hear at the end.
Explain why the -ent stays in writing.
line: Why {ils veulent} ends in -ent on the page but not out loud.

parts.heading: Say it without the -ent
text: With {ils} and {elles}, most French verbs end in -ent. You write those three letters, but you do not say them.
Stop the word right before the -ent. {ils veulent} sounds like eel vuhl.
parts.note: The s of {ils} and {elles} is silent here as well, because {veulent} starts with a consonant. The t of -ent comes back only in a few liaisons, such as in some questions.

parts.heading: One person or more
text: Compare one person with more than one. In {veulent} you hear an l at the end. In {veut} you do not.
parts.note: In many verbs you will meet later, the two forms sound exactly alike. Then only the spelling shows that more than one person is doing it.

parts.heading: Silent, but still written
text: The -ent marks the plural, as the s does in {amis}. You see it on the page, but you do not hear it.
French children learn this rule at school when they are seven or eight.
parts.note: In the present, a few very common verbs end in -ont instead, such as {ils sont} and {ils ont}. In those, you do hear the vowel of the ending.

parts.heading: How the ending went quiet
text: People once said this ending out loud. It went quiet one sound at a time, over several hundred years, while the spelling stayed the same.
parts.note: One of the first books to record the silent n was written in English, for English speakers learning French. Even in the 1700s, some older people in the French countryside still said the ending. Many French letters that are written but not said have a story like this one.

list: In Latin, the ending was spoken.
In the French of the Middle Ages, people still said it.
In the 1500s, grammar books said the n was no longer heard. Some speakers still said the t before a pause.
In the 1600s, the t went quiet too.
Today, the ending is written but usually not said.
blocks.heading: A little at a time

checks.ask: Listen. Which one did you hear?
checks.why: You heard an l at the end, so it was {ils veulent}. The -ent adds no sound.

checks.ask: Listen. In {elles veulent}, which endings are silent?
checks.why: {veulent} starts with a consonant, so the s of {elles} stays silent. The -ent is silent too.

options.text: It shows that more than one person is doing it
It tells you to say a t at the end
It shows that the action is in the past

checks.why: The ending went quiet hundreds of years ago, but it stayed in the spelling. On the page it marks the plural, as the s does in {amis}.
